content: Preterm birth is responsible for 60% to 80% of neonatal deaths. Among the infants who survive, many face lifelong complications. Maternal infections are implicated in 30% to 50% of preterm labor cases. Probiotics are defined as live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, provide health benefits to the host. These microorganisms have demonstrated the ability to displace and eliminate pathogens, as well as modulate the immune response. This suggests that probiotics may interfere with the inflammatory processes that contribute to preterm labor and delivery. During pregnancy, treatments that restore normal vaginal flora and acidity locally, without systemic effects, may be preferable for preventing preterm labor. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of probiotics in preventing preterm labor and birth. A search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register on February 20, 2010. The selection criteria included all randomized controlled trials that assessed the prevention of preterm birth in pregnant women, or women planning pregnancy, through the use of probiotics to treat or prevent urogenital infections. The quality of the trials was independently assessed by all review authors, and data were extracted accordingly. Seven trials were evaluated for inclusion in the review, and three trials were ultimately included. The effects of probiotics on very preterm birth (defined as less than 32 weeks of gestation) showed a risk ratio (RR) of 0.65 with a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 0.03 to 15.88. For preterm birth (defined as less than 37 weeks of gestation), the RR was 3.95 with a 95% CI ranging from 0.36 to 42.91. These results demonstrated very wide confidence intervals and no statistically significant effects (based on one trial involving 238 women). The effects of probiotics on neonatal death or severe morbidity could not be estimated due to insufficient data. The impact of probiotics on vaginal infections was assessed in two trials involving a total of 88 women. The use of probiotics was associated with an 81% reduction in the risk of genital infections, with a risk ratio of 0.19 and a 95% confidence interval ranging from 0.08 to 0.48. In conclusion, while probiotics appear to be effective in treating vaginal infections during pregnancy, there is currently insufficient evidence from trials to demonstrate any significant impact on the prevention of preterm birth or its associated complications.
